title: The Gift Card Lands in December. The Debt It Creates Doesn't Clear Until It's Redeemed.
excerpt: A gift card sale lands in your account looking exactly like profit. Until it's redeemed, it's a liability you still have to deliver on, often in a quieter month with thinner margin.
content:
A gift card sells itself. No stock to pick, no delivery to arrange, no service to deliver on the day. The customer pays, the till rings it up, and the money lands in the account looking exactly like every other sale that month. For a lot of retail, hospitality, salon and gym businesses across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, gift cards turn into one of the strongest income lines of the entire year through late November and December.

That is also where the trap sits. A gift card sale is not a completed sale. It is a promise to hand over goods or a service at some point in the future, and the cash collected today is only a deposit against that promise. The pattern we typically see is that the bank balance rises in December and gets treated as if it was already earned profit, spent on Christmas stock, bonuses or debt repayment, when a meaningful share of it is still owed to a customer who has not walked back in the door yet.

None of this is a bookkeeping failure. Your bookkeeper is almost certainly recording gift card proceeds exactly the way the accounting standards require, as a liability rather than revenue, until the card is redeemed or expires. The gap sits in how the owner reads the number on internet banking day to day, not in how the ledger records it.

A Sale That Isn't a Sale Yet

Under standard accounting treatment, money collected for a gift card is deferred revenue. It sits on the balance sheet as a liability, an obligation to deliver something of equal value later, and only converts to actual revenue on the profit and loss statement once the card is redeemed. That distinction matters because most owner-led businesses do not check their financial position through the balance sheet. They check it through the bank account, and a bank account cannot tell the difference between money that is genuinely available and money that is already spoken for.

The businesses that get caught out are rarely the ones selling the most gift cards. They are the ones whose day to day cash decisions, what stock to order, what wages to commit to, whether to bring forward a piece of equipment, get made off the total bank balance rather than off the balance minus the outstanding gift card liability.

Where the Redemption Lands

Gift card redemption rarely mirrors the sales pattern. Cards sell heavily through December, but they get redeemed across a much longer window, through January, February and often well beyond, since Australian Consumer Law generally requires gift cards to remain valid for a minimum of three years from the date of purchase. Some of that liability sits on the books for a long time before it is ever called in.

The redemption window that catches most owners is the near-term one. A card sold at full price in December often gets redeemed during the January clearance period, when the stock being handed over is marked down and the margin the business actually earns on that redemption is thinner than the margin it assumed when the card was sold. A hospitality venue that sells a voucher for a festive set menu in December may see it redeemed in February for a dish with a higher food cost percentage once seasonal produce prices shift. The cash collected does not change. What it actually covers does.

Forecasting the Liability Instead of Spending the Balance

The fix is not to stop selling gift cards. They are a genuinely useful source of upfront cash and a reasonable way to bring forward future trade. The fix is to treat the outstanding gift card balance as a forecast line rather than folding it into the general cash position. A running total of unredeemed liability, built from actual sales and a realistic redemption rate drawn from the point of sale or booking system, gives a much more honest picture of what is actually available to spend versus what is already owed.

This is precisely the kind of visibility a 13-Week Cash Flow Build is built to surface, mapping known obligations like gift card redemptions alongside supplier payments and wage commitments so the forecast reflects what the business can actually spend, not just what happens to be sitting in the account on a given Tuesday. For businesses layering a strong December on top of normal trading, that distinction is often the difference between a comfortable January and a tight one.

Most owners do not need to change how they sell gift cards. They need a clearer line between the cash that has landed and the cash that is still owed against a future delivery. A fractional CFO working alongside your existing bookkeeping typically picks this pattern up in the first month of engagement, simply by asking what the gift card liability balance actually is rather than assuming the bank balance already accounts for it. If your business runs a meaningful gift card or voucher program heading into this Christmas, book a discovery call and we can look at what portion of December's cash is actually free to spend.

faqs.q: Is gift card income counted as revenue as soon as it is sold?
faqs.a: No. Under standard accounting treatment, money collected for a gift card is recorded as a liability, not revenue, because the business still owes the customer goods or a service of equal value. It only converts to revenue once the card is redeemed. This is standard practice and exactly what a competent bookkeeper should be doing with that income.

faqs.q: Why does a strong December in gift card sales still cause a tight January?
faqs.a: Because the cash lands in December but a share of it is already committed to deliveries that haven't happened yet. If that cash gets spent as though it was already earned profit, the business can find itself short when customers start redeeming cards through January and February, often during a quieter trading period with less fresh cash coming in to cover the gap.

faqs.q: How long are gift cards valid for under Australian law?
faqs.a: Australian Consumer Law generally requires most gift cards to remain valid for a minimum of three years from the date of purchase. That means a meaningful share of outstanding gift card liability can sit on a business's books for an extended period before it is ever redeemed, which is worth factoring into longer-term cash planning rather than assuming it clears within the same financial year.

faqs.q: Should a small business track gift card liability separately from its cash balance?
faqs.a: Yes. Reviewing the outstanding gift card liability as its own running total, alongside a realistic redemption rate from the point of sale system, gives a far more accurate picture of what cash is genuinely free to spend. Building this into a cash flow discipline practice is a simple way to stop the bank balance being treated as the whole picture.

faqs.q: Why can redeeming a gift card during a sale period cost more than expected?
faqs.a: A card sold at full price in December is sometimes redeemed during a January clearance or discount period, when the product or service being handed over carries a thinner margin than it did at the time of sale. The cash collected stays the same, but what it actually needs to cover has shifted, which is why the margin on redemption deserves its own attention rather than assuming it matches the margin at sale.

faqs.q: How does a 13-week cash flow forecast handle gift card redemptions?
faqs.a: A 13-Week Cash Flow Build maps known obligations, including expected gift card redemptions, against upcoming supplier payments and wage commitments, so the forecast reflects what can genuinely be spent rather than the raw bank balance. For businesses with a meaningful voucher or gift card program, this is often the first place a hidden cash gap shows up.

faqs.q: Does a fractional CFO typically pick up gift card liability as an issue?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a common early finding. A fractional CFO reviewing the business for the first time will usually ask what the outstanding gift card or voucher liability actually is, separate from the general cash position, because that distinction is rarely visible from day to day banking alone, and it often reshapes how the owner reads every bank balance afterwards.
